claim: Denning and Buzen 1978: a closed system saturates at N* = R0/(Vb Sb) jobs, called the saturation point, where R0 is the sum of visit ratio times service time over all devices and Vb Sb is the bottleneck demand; throughput is capped at 1/(Vb Sb). Analytic, no measured gain.
note: Read from a course-hosted copy with a damaged cross-reference table; the formula is garbled in the text layer.

claim: Denning and Buzen 1978: with think time Z, queueing is certain once there are more than Mb* = (R0 + Z)/(Vb Sb) terminals, which equals N* + Mb. Analytic, no measured gain.
Denning and Buzen 1978: a large improvement at the bottleneck device moves the bottleneck to another device (analytic statement, no measurement).
note: The paper line is approximate (about line 1035 of the text file).

claim: Denning and Buzen 1978: the saturation point holds only while visit ratios and mean service times do not change as N grows; job-flow balance is also assumed.

Lazowska 1984 (chapter 5): a closed network's throughput obeys N/(N D + Z) <= X(N) <= min(N/(D + Z), 1/Dmax), with D the total demand, Dmax the bottleneck demand and Z the think time. Analytic bounds, no measured gain.
Lazowska 1984 (chapter 5): the throughput bounds rest on a single assumption, that a customer's service demand at a centre does not depend on how many others are in the system or where they are.

Lazowska 1984 (chapter 6): the exact mean-value recursion applies only to networks of load-independent and delay centres, but the authors report that its accuracy is very robust to violating this assumption.
note: The robustness is the authors' experience, not a measurement made here. The algorithm itself was not read.

claim: Sztrik 2001 (lecture slides, citing Kleinrock vol. II): for one server with general service time b and generation time 1/lambda, the saturation number is N* = (b + 1/lambda)/b.
note: Secondary text: the cited Kleinrock volume was not opened.

claim: Sztrik 2001 (lecture slides, citing Kleinrock): if service and generation times are exactly fixed, N* is the maximum number of messages that can be scheduled without mutual interference.
note: Secondary text: the cited Kleinrock volume was not opened.

claim: Holtman and Gunther 2008: in the standard machine-repairman model throughput cannot be retrograde (fall as N grows) for any N, S or Z; the Universal Scalability Law corresponds to synchronous queueing in a load-dependent machine-repairman model.
Holtman and Gunther 2008: synchronous queueing gives the worst-case throughput and so represents a lower bound on throughput (cited in the paper as ZSEG82).

Desruelle 1994: for a machine-repairman network with general service and delay times and at most 15 customers, the approximation's absolute error is at most 15% for a service-to-delay ratio from 0.1 to 4; the relative error is under 20% at fifteen customers and under 10% below seven customers.
note: The error comparison is against simulation, as the collect file states; the derivation was not read.

claim: Holman, Chaudhry and Ghosal 1981: for an open bulk-service queue with Poisson arrivals, traffic intensity 0.9, capacity B = 5 and service shape k = 1, the tabulated mean queue size falls only from 27.126 (quorum A = 1) to 25.009 (quorum A = 5) customers.
note: Open queue with an unlimited population, not a finite-source result; tabulated values only, derivation not read.

claim: Sztrik 2004 (book): for one server the saturation number is again N* = (b + 1/lambda)/b, described as the maximum number of messages that can be scheduled without mutual interference (citing Kleinrock).
note: Same formula as the slides in x30-0307; a second source for it, not an independent test.
